doc.title: George Avakian interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 21, 1998

title: Pop albums, International Department and the LP
summary: Avakian ran pop albums and the International Department, helped produce the first LPs, and saw overseas markets grow.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: people there who don’t really have that much interest in music, no matter how much they talk about it. But the big thing is that having had this miniature exposure as it grew, I got exposed more and more to what was happening in the New York club scene and so forth, and recording wise I wasn’t too keen on getting into it. Well first of all you have to remember that in ‘47, a year after I got into the record business, I was not only just a junior producer of the pop singles of the day, there wasn’t any album business to speak of, but Mr. Wallerstein put me in charge of popular albums and also when the director of the International Department retired at sixty some-odd, I was put in charge of that department too because of my foreign background and interest in standard music, you know the music of Gershwin, and Porter and Youmans and so forth. That was valuable in running the pop album department. And of course my interest in foreign music and my knowledge of languages made me a natural for the International Department. Now you have to remember both departments were microscopic. That’s why I was given those jobs. Nobody else wanted them. But Mr. Wallenstein knew that they were trying to develop a long playing records, and when they did in ‘48, 50 years ago, I was sitting in a remarkable position. Between us Howard Scott, who was another young producer in the Masterworks Department, and I produced the first 100 pop and 100 classical LPs and we never knew that it was going to be so big. It got to be big of course in classical music right away. But on the pop side, the ten-inch LP was not too meaningful because it was not an album business for popular music. It became that in ‘53, and I won’t describe the process because there are many factors which had nothing to do with music, which made a twelve-inch pop LP so big in terms of sales volume and interest by the public, and of course the changes in what was recorded and how it was presented to the public, that it totally revised the way the record business was run on the pop side. Instead of the emphasis being just on single records and pop hits to drive the pop sales, and the activity of recording pop music, it became a packaging concept with all kinds of — if I may say so — much higher quality content than the hit single of the day philosophy, which was the force behind the pop record business until LP started to take over. The international side grew enormously because of this. The foreign affiliates that American companies had were not too interested in most of the classical music because the classical music market in Europe was so much bigger than pop music was, compared to the way it was in America, so they didn’t need to have very much in the way of classical music coming over from the United States. The pop performers that they preferred were people that they had seen in movies like Frank Sinatra and Doris Day. But then the burgeoning interest in jazz that had already begun before the war created a market for jazz LPs in Europe which was quickly fed by jazz musicians going to Europe, which was not an ordinary thing until air travel really got established in the early 50s. And from then on, the American pop © Fillius Jazz Archive -16-

albums became more and more important in Europe and finally Japan. When I left Columbia Records in 1958, Europe was bringing in almost as much money in the album sales to the American originators as the domestic sales were. And when Japan got on board, which was really about 1960 I would say, Japan ended up being bigger than Europe. Now all of this international business was made possible through the long playing record, and jazz was an important part of it. It isn’t anymore and hasn’t been for many years because the rock musicians in England helped change that, the interest in jazz began dropping off. But to this day jazz musicians make a better living playing in Japan and Europe than they do in the United States, which is a tragic thing but that’s the way it is.
